caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 119 of 1999 with CR 349 (FM) 1999
lawyer:
Md Mostafa, Advocate — For the Appellants. 
Gazi Sayedul Haque, Advocate — For the Respondents.
parties:
President, Magura Town Hall & another ------ Appellant
vs
President, Magura District Ainjibi Samity and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J: This appeal is directed against the order dated 5-5-99 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Magura in Title Suit No. 2 of 1999 on the plaintiff''s application for temporary injunction under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure directing the parties to maintain status quo in respect of possession in the suit property till the disposal of the appeal.

2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that, respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Magura being Title Suit No. 2 of 1999, praying for declaration of title in the suit property and for recovery of Khas possession therein. After filing the suit the plaintiff filed an application praying for temporary injunction under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure restraining the defendants from making any act of reconstruction or further constructions in the suit property or from in any way changing the nature and character thereof till the disposal of the suit. The plaintiff''s case, in short, is that the Magura Bar Association by organizing an amateur Dramatic Club founded Magura Theatre in 1918 for fostering cultural activities in the locality. It has been alleged that Mr Charu Chandra Sen, the Secretary of the plaintiff Samity, was the founding secretary of the Magura Theatre and it was so recorded in his name in CS Khatian No. 377 and SA Khatian No. 386. It has also been alleged that for convenience of management the plaintiff Samity subsequently made over the Magura Theatre to defendant Magura Town Club for running the same under the control and supervision of the plaintiff. It has been also alleged that it was settled between the parties that defendant Magura Town Hall would rebuild an auditorium at its own cost on the plan approved by the plaintiff. It has been further contended that long since the plaintiff Samity has been deputing at least two of its members to the Executive Committee of the Magura Town Club for looking after the interests of the plaintiff Samity. It has also been alleged that the plaintiff Samity leased out the suit property to the Magura Talkie, The Modhumita Cinema Hall and other establishments as licensees under the plaintiff and it has been realising rent from the tenants. It has been further alleged that as the Magura Town Club and its Auditorium became old and dilapidated and ultimately it was decided in February, 1998 that the Magura Town Hall Auditorium would be pulled down for the purpose of reconstruction and development on the plan approved by the plaintiff Samity and the construction works would be carried out under the direct supervision and control of the Samity, and a contractor was engaged for the purpose. At this stage the defendant illegally claimed the suit property and the suit and prayer for temporary injunction.

3. Other Class Suit No. 104 of 1998 was filed before the Sadar Assistant Judge, Magura. In that suit the plaintiff obtained an order of temporary injunction against the defendant restraining it from making any construction work in the suit premises until further orders. Thereafter the defendant appeared in that suit and raised the question of jurisdiction of the Court on the ground of valuation of the suit whereupon the learned Assistant Judge found the suit beyond his pecuniary jurisdiction and on such finding returned the plaint to the filing Advocate for presentation before the appropriate Court following which it has subsequent been filed before the Subordinate Magura.

4. The respondent as defendant resisted the aforesaid application for temporary injunction denying all its material allegations and contended, inter alia, that the plaintiff has no prima facie arguable case for injunction it has been contended that the CS Khatian stands in the name of Charu Chandra Sen as Secretary of Magura Town Hall and not as the Secretary of Magura Ainjibi Samity. It has also been asserted that Mr Charu Chandra Sen, although was a lawyer and a member of the plaintiff Samity, he was never the Secretary of the plaintiff Samity at any point of time and all assertion to the contrary are false and concocted. It has been further asserted that the finally published SA Khatian also stands in the name of Advocate Charu Chandra Sen as the Secretary of Magura Town Hall and not as the Secretary of Magura Bar Association as alleged by the plaintiff. It was stated that by a resolution passed in 1953 at the instance of the then SDO, Magura Theatre was renamed as Magura Town Hall and constitution was adopted for the Magura Town Club making provision for taking two members from the local Bar Association to the Executive Committee of the defendant Club as a matter of convenience but not as a matter of compulsion. It has been also asserted that by a regular resolution duly approved in the general meeting of the members of the defendant Samity the decision for reconstruction and development was taken and a construction Sub-Committee containing two members from the local Bar Association was formed in keeping with the previous practice. It has been stated that by registered Kabuliyat dated 23-1-18 the defendant took lease of the suit property in the name of Advocate Charu Chandra Sen clearly describing him as the Secretary of Magura Theatre subsequently renamed as Magura Town Club and not as the Secretary of Magura Ainjibi Samity. It has been alleged that Magura Town Hall is being run, managed and administered in accordance with its constitution, which was finally adopted in 1980 and nobody, including the plaintiff, ever took any exception to it at any point of time. It has been further alleged that in pursuance of the resolution dated 24-10-97, duly approved by the General Meeting of the defendant Club to the effect that a modern shopping complex be constructed in the suit premises a sub-committee was duly formed for supervision of the construction work and tender was invited from intending contractors, the lowest tender was ultimately accepted and work order was given in pursuance thereof. It has also been contended that the rent from the existing eight shops standing in the suit premises amounting to Taka 6,400.00 is being spent towards payment of salary to the clerk, peon, sweeper and towards payment of water rates, electricity charges and the like income and expenditure of the defendant Club are being properly maintained and audited. It has been further contended that the Magura Pourasava duly approved the plan submitted by the defendant and the on-going construction work is being carried on accordingly. It has been contended that more than Taka 1,10,001.00 has already been spent in the on-going construction work and the order of ad-interim injunction has already caused heavy losses and injury to the defendant Club and if an order of temporary injunction is passed against the defendant, the entire project will be destroyed causing irreparable loss and injury to the defendant. It was asserted that the balance of convenience and inconvenience stands heavily against the plaintiff and in favour of the contesting defendant.

The point for determination:

5. The only point for determination in the appeal is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in passing the order of status quo in respect of possession in the suit property, which, in reality, is an order of injunction in the case?

Findings and decisions:

<u>6. It appears from the impugned order that the learned Subordinate Judge on detailed discussion and consideration of the materials placed before him clearly found that the plaintiff does not have any prima facie arguable case for temporary injunction. On the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge clearly found in the impugned judgment itself that the defendant has prima facie title and possession in the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the plaintiff has failed to produce even a scrap of paper in support of its case while the contesting defendant has produced heaps of documentary evidence supporting its claim over the suit property. The CS Khatian and the SA Khatian in respect of the suit property fully support the case of the defendant and this position is further strengthened by payment of rent by the defendant to the Government Acquired Estate. It is unfortunate that the learned Subordinate Judge after having recorded such clear finding suddenly turned about and allowed the application for temporary injunction by directing the parties to maintain status quo on illegal and irrelevant considerations. The order of status quo in this case virtually means an order of injunction against the ongoing construction work in the suit property at the instance of the contesting defendant</u>

<u>7. Law on temporary injunction is by now well settled. It has been consistently held by the superior Court of the country that in order to be entitled to an order of temporary injunction the applicant must prove three things: (a) a prima facie case in his favour, (b) he shall suffer irreparable loss and injury if injunction is refused to him and (c) the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in his favour and it is against the defendant. In the instant case, all the considerations regulating the grant of temporary injunction stand out prominently against the plaintiff and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge clearly erred in law in granting temporary injunction in the form of status quo against the settled principle of law. The approach of the learned Subordinate Judge must be deprecated as being patently illegal and arbitrary and devoid of judicial norms.</u>

8. Mr Gazi Sayedul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for Mr Abul Khair on behalf of the respondent, submits that since the learned trial Court passed an order directing the parties to maintain status quo in respect of the suit property, it is necessary in the interest of justice that the said order be maintained, otherwise, unnecessary complications shall arise. As we have already found that the order of status quo in this case verily amounts to an order of injunction against the defendant from carrying on the construction work in progress. We find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

9. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, we find substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant and accordingly, these are sustained.

10. In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs and the impugned order of status quo dated 5-5-99 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Magura in Title Suit No. 2 of 1999 is set aside. The cost is assessed at Taka 1000.00 only (taka one thousand).

11. The learned Subordinate Judge is hereby directed to dispose of Title Suit No. 2 of 1999 as expeditiously as possible, preferably within six months from the date of receipt of the order. The connected Rule being CR 349 (FM) 99 is accordingly, made absolute.

Communicate the order to the learned Subordinate Judge Magura immediately.

End.
